That illustrates what I mean by the position with regard to education. A second chamber, in my humble opinion was thought necessary at that time, probably more than for any other reason, because of the want of education, and ability in the people to intelligently and successfully deal with the important matters that parliament has to deal with. That being the position, I wish to say that I do not concede at all that because we had a second chamber at the time of confederation there is any reason for continuing it. j wish to emphasize the j fact that at the time of confederation the I conditions in this country were entirely i different from what they are now. I do not concede in any way that anything is to | be said against this resolution from the i mere fact that the second chamber was | established forty years ago. I do not be-| lieve that if our ancesters had realized 1 at the time confederation was brought I about that in a few years this country \ would have attained to the state of education at which it has arrived to-day they ' Mr. LANCASTER.
would have concluded that there should be] a permanent second chamber, i Then, the* condition of things is entirely different. Having regard to the condition at that time they felt it was necessary to safeguard the constitution by having a second chamber not elected directly by the people.
I suppose their reason was that they thought that the comparative ignorance of the ordinary voter might result in the creation of a sentiment in the country which would intimidate or frighten members of parliament into doing something that was altogether too radical, and not in the true interest of the. country, un-British and ill-advised. Therefore, they sought to provide the check which the British constitution gives in the home land in the form of cooling chamber, so as to speak. Their object no doubt was, looking at the matter from the standpoint of the people of Canada, to prevent, by any popular or sudden declaration of public opinion, the adoption of a course that might bring about disaster to the country. The reason for having a second chamber in Great Britain is very different from what it is in this country. People who say there is the same necessity for a Senate in Canada as there is for a House of Lords in England are speaking without realizing what they are talking about. The House of Lords in England is the only safeguard between the Commons and the King, and if the House of Lords were not there the Commons would be able to force the King to abdicate if he did not give way whenever the elective chamber choose to ask his assent to any particular line of policy. There is no other safeguard, or bulwark, or cooling basin to put a check upon hasty legislation in Great Britain but the House of Lords. But, in this country,. if the House of Commons, notwithstanding all that I have hinted at with regard to education to-day as compared with the state of education in the days when confederation was brought about, were to pass hasty legislation under which certain interests were injured, under which the rights of minorities were interfered with unfairly or unconstitutionally,' or was tending in that direction, or if even without unconstitutional legislation the rights of minorities were interfered with, for the checking of which the second chamber is supposed to exist, I say, and I wish to emphasise this point, that the second chamber would be useless. By the constitution under which we live any Bill passed by this parliament is subject to disallowance whether there be a Senate or not. Whether the Senate exists or whether it does not exist, every Bill adopted by this parliament has to be passed upon under the constitution by the home authorities within two years and it can be, without any wrench to the constitution, abrogated, set aside, and, annulled as if it were just

so much waste paper. There are a great many gentlemen both in this House and out of the House-more out of the House- who do not appear to be well informed upon this point who are not aware of this fact, and as ' Hansard ' is a public document that every person can obtain I think it is well that I should put upon ' Hansard ' the sections of the British North America Act which I referred to in a previous debate on this subject last session, and which every one, who chooses to obtain a copy of ' Hansard,' can read for himself. Section 55 of the British North America Act under which we exist to-day as a parliament says this :
Where a Bill passed by the Houses of the parliament is presented to the Governor General for the Queen's assent, he shall declare according to his discretion, but subject to the provisions of this Act and to Her Majesty's instructions, either that he assents thereto in the Queen's name, or that he withholds the Queen's assent, or that he reserves the Bill for the signification of the Queen's pleasure.
Section 56,
Where the Governor General assents to a Bill in the Queen's name, he shall by the first convenient opportunity send an authentic copy of the Act to one of Her Majesty's principal Secretaries of State, and if the Queen in Council within two years after receipt thereof by the Secretary of State thinks fit to disallow the Act, such disallowance (with a certificate of the Secretary of State of the day on which the Act was received by him) being justified by the Governor General, by speech or message to each of the Houses of the parliament or by proclamation, shall annul the Act from and after the day of such signification.
Then section 57,
A Bill reserved for the signification of the Queen's pleasure shall not have any force unless and until within two years from the day on which it was presented to the Governor General for the Queen's assent, the Governor General signifies, by speech or message to each of the Houses of the parliament or by proclamation, that it has received the assent of the Queen in Council.
Then it says:
An entry of every such speech, message or proclamation shall be made in the Journal of the House.	[DOT]
I need not read that as it does not affect the sense. Under these sections, and more particularly under section 56, after a Bill has been passed by both Houses of this parliament as at present constituted, and notwithstanding that the Senate has approved of the Bill the assent of His Excellency to that Bill has no permanent effect, because the King in council in Great Britain, can within two years, if they see fit, disallow that Bill. Of course that would not often happen and if it did I would not be petitioning the King to abolish the
Senate, because I would feel that there might be some need indirectly for the existence of that body. What I point out is that whatever action the Senate may take on a Bill, whether it rejects our Bill or whether it amends it or whether it forces us to concur in their amendments, after all, that Bill may be refused by the home government and the constitution of this country is in no way wrenched. It would be no reflection upon His Excellency-because his very appointment is a limited power of attorney in such matters if I may be pardoned for using the expression-if after he assented to that Bill it should be rejected by the home government. Now, supposing we had no Senate, is not what I have just indicated all the protection that is required for the various interests the Senate is supposed to protect. No Bill has ever been discussed in this House that has not found men here to point out that it infringes on vested interests, if that be the case. The members returned to this House have to recognize vested interests, and every other interest and if any of us were to advocate in this House an attack on these interests which the second chamber is supposed to guard, the chances are that we would not be re-elected. If any interests be disastrously affected by our legislation, these interests have in a sense control over members of parliament, and if a member of parliament be extreme or-unreasonable on any point the chances are that he would not again be returned to the House. A man may come to this House of Commons biassed, but he hears the debates and discussions, and he gradually becomes more reasonable. He may fight for principles and point out why they should be put into practice, but the tendency is that the men who come here are educated by their fellow members, and the result is that the Commons does not pass legislation against any interests that may require protection from the second chamber. The need for a second chamber today is in an entirely different position from what it was in 1867. If a Bill of an extremely radical character were passed by this House-one of the kind the Senate is supposed to protect the country against- and if the Senate assented to it, would any one say that if that legislation were calculated to work havoc in this country, that the interests affected could not go to Great Britain and seek its disallowance. Surely, if it were not important and weighty enough to pursue with regard to it such a course as that provided in section 56, the interests affected could not be very much hurt. Let me give an instance of how the Senate as at present constituted may be a barrier to carrying into legislation the wishes of the people. I regret I have to refer to a personal matter and to speak of a Bill which I had a great deal to do with. For seven years I sought in this House to

Using the same sort of argument, I would say, with all deference to the Prime Minister, is it not equally plain that, if the House of Commons has so acted as not to require the Senate to protect minorities, that is a reason why no Senate was needed to protect minorities? Going on with the history of what public men have done about the Senate, let me point out that this constitution was not in existence 20 years before murmur-ings began to arise concerning the Senate. This murmuring increased to such an extent that 17 years ago one of the great political parties of the country, at a convention held in Ottawa in 1893, passed the following resolution in regard to it:
The present constitution of the Senate is inconsistent with the federal principle in out-system of government, and is in other respects defective, as it makes the Senate independent of the people, and uncontrolled by public opinion of the country, and should be so amended as to bring it into harmony with the principles of popular government.
Now. two things stand out prominently in that resolution. That great political party declared that the Senate was inconsistent with federal principles 'and that it was in other respects defective, and it pledged itself, on going into power, to remedy those defects. From that time to this there have been various agitations on this Subject in the country, but the govern-

Mr. Speaker, when you left the Chair at six o'clock, I was pointing out what seemed to me to be instances of the lack of usefulness of the Senate in making legislation in this country during the last ten years. In this connection I would point out that nearly every public man of standing in the Liberal party has, at one time or another, some of them many times, during the last ten or fifteen years, stated many objections to our present system of legislation, owing to the inefficiency or worse of the Senate. For instance two years ago Senator Sir Richard Scott, almost immediately after he had ceased to be a member of the present cabinet-and I do not know whether that fact has any significance-made one of the most emphatic utterances in condemnation of the present system of appointment to the Senate, and introduced in that chamber a motion seeking to reform it. His motion was to this effect:
That in the opinion of the Senate the time lias arrived for so amending the constitution of this branch of parliament as to bring the mode of selection of senators more into harmony with public opinion.
This is a clear and distinct statement by a senator of many years' standing that he recognizes that the Senate is not at all in harmony with public opinion, and reading between the lines it is easy to understand from his language that he believed the constitution must be so amended as to make the Senate of more use to the country. Sir Richard Scott supported this motion earnestly. He suggested as a mode of appointment the election of two-thirds of the members of the Senate by the people and the appointment of one-third by the Crown, for seven years in each case. His suggestion did not meet with very much favour, in fact no suggestion for the reform of the Senate has ever met with strong support from any large number of people. One gentleman will propose one reform, another a different reform, some newspaper a third, but, practically speaking, no plan receives the support of any person except the proposer of the reform. In fact, although the large majority of the people and of the members of parliament believe that, as Sir Richard Scott says, the Senate must be reformed, no two people will agree as to what reform should be made. The Prime Minister will remember that three years ago, speaking on the motion of the present
deputy Speaker (Mr. McIntyre) for the reform of the Senate, the right hon. gentleman pointed out just what I have said. He discussed seriatim all the reforms that have been suggested and decided that not one of them was acceptable. The Prime* Minister has not himself suggested any method of reform. By the Liberal platform of 1893 he and his party were pledged to the reform of the Senate. The Prime Minister is a man of great ability and ingenuity who is never without means to accomplish what he thinks ought to be accomplished in the interests of this country, yet since 1896, for nearly fifteen years, the Prime Minister has had it within his power as Prime Minister to introduce some of the reforms to which he pledged himself in 1893 and on which he attained office in 1896. If the Prime Minister, holding office under that pledge, with all his ability, his vast resources of mind, and his great power, has not been able to effect a reform, it is fair and reasonable to take the position that the Senate is not working properly and in the interests of the country, that it cannot be reformed, and that it should be abolished. Therefore, I believe the concrete motion I have brought forward, which takes the form of an humble petition to His Gracious Majesty to so amend the British North America Act as to provide for the abolition of the Senate, is the only sensible, practical, reasonable action for this House to take under the circumstances. To assume otherwise is to assume that while the Prime Minister with - the vast majority he has had since 1896, with all his power, with all his ability having been unable to effect a reform, some of us can do what he cannot do, an assumption which is ridiculous.
In view of all these circumstances one must come to the conclusion that the only sensible, practical and reasonable thing to do is to petition the imperial parliament tp provide for the abolition of the Senate as an entirely unnecessary body.
Other prominent members of the Liberal party vigorously followed up the pledge contained in the platform of 1895. Sir Richard Cartwright, another member of the Senate, was one of the most emphatic speakers on this question. He has been, from the beginning, a member of the present administration. He was one of the leading Liberals of the country in 1893, and was present at that convention. When this plank was made in the party platform, he expected-and, as it turned out, rightly expected-to be a member of the cabinet if his party attained power. He sat for years in this House as a member of the government and deskmate of the Prime Minister, and it is only a few years ago that he was translated to the upper cham-1 ber, where he sits still as a member of the

government. This hon. gentleman, in 1896, following up what he understood to be the opinion of the Liberal party-and you cannot blame me if I think the same as he did-t'haj the Senate should, be abolished, **and speaking in Massey Hall, Toronto, dealt with this question of the Senate. Remember, he had had three years since 1893 in which to thoroughly consider and understand what the platform of 1893 meant. And I have his words before me. I put them on ' Hansard ' last year, but it will do no harm to refresh the minds of hon. gentlemen opposite on this subject. He said:-
The Senate was a millstone around the neok of the Canadian people which he prayed that Providence would soon remove.
If he is still praying, the locality from which he offers his prayers, I should think, would prevent them from doing much good. I doubt if his prayers go through the roof, for he occupies a place in the very institution for the abolition of which he was praying in 1896. Speaking seriously to the people on the eve of a general election, speaking as right-hand man and prospective colleague of the leader whom he wished to see placed in power, trying to convince the people that his party should be put in power, he declared the Senate to be a millstone around the neck of the Canadian people, which he prayed that Providence would soon remove. How he was ever able to take a seat in the Senate after that I do not know, but since he has been in the Senate I have not heard of him offering up that prayer. If there was cause in 1896, why this august body, the Senate, should be removed, in the opinion of Sir Richard Cartwright and of the present Prime Minister, what has happened since then to justify a change of their opinion?
Now, the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) may ~ not have intended to say quite what he did say in answer to me when I spoke on this subject last session. What he said will be found at page 2054 of ' Hansard.' He spoke in part as follows:-
It may be that the present action of the Senate is not satisfactory to my hon. friend (Mr. Lancaster). I can remember when the action of the Senate as it existed twenty years ago was not very satisfactory to me, for instance. My scruples are not the same to-day as they were then, and it may be that the time will come when my hon. friend will change his views on this point, and, the composition of the Senate being different, his objection may be removed. But he says that, as no satisfactory reform of the Senate is suggested, there is a general opinion that the condition of the Senate at the present time is not satisfactory and that all heartily desire a change. I agree that there has been a strong suggestion made at different times and in different quarters that we should have a reform of the Senate.

What does that mean? I can only take one meaning from it, and that is that when the majority of members of the Senate were of a different stripe from the right hon. gentleman it was a bad Senate, but since, by the effluxion of time and, other causes, a majority of the Senate is now made up of his friends, and largely of his own appointees, his objection is removed. I hope that was not his meaning, because it would be no answer to my argument. It is such an argument as no independent-minded man would consider for a moment. But there has been no change in the Senate except in the political complexion of the majority. I regret if I have taken the wrong meaning from what the right hon. gentleman said; if I am wrong, I hope he will put me right. Rut I am forced to the conclusion that the reason why the opinion of the, right hon. gentleman has changed in the last twenty,years is that the political complexion of the Senate to-day is different, from what it was twenty years ago. I can assure the right hon. gentleman that' my grievance against the Senate is not, merely that the political complexion off the Senate does not please me. My objection to them is that very often they do nothing to help the country to secure good legislation, and when they do wake up, they wake up at the wrong time, obstruct good legislation passed by this House, and so do mischief.
There was another hon. gentleman who, in his lifetime was very highly respected, now gone to his reward

Sir' Oliver Mowat. He was everywhere respected for! his ability as a public man. He also, joined the cabinet of the right hon. Prime Minister, becoming his Minister of Justice. In 1896 he was active in trying to get the present Prime Minister placed in power, and he, like others, spoke on the subject of the Senate. I placed one of his remarks on 1 Hansard ' last year, but it will do no harm to repeat it and so remind hon. members of what was said. It will be found at page 2042 of ' Hansard'' of last year:
We are agreed as to the necessity of a fundamental reform of the Senate, if, for any reason, it must or should be retained.
The pith of that sentence-yes, and its sting-are in the last clause, ' if, for any reason, it must or should be retained.' It is quite clear that Sir Oliver Mowat thought that there was no need of it at all. Sir Oliver Mowat thought there was no need of it at all, at most he would compromise on a reform of the Senate, and he took care to say: We are all agreed. That is, all the leading members of his party who were going to form a cabinet after they got into power, as they did in 1896, were agreed that something must be done. Now

we must assume in all fairness to this government that they have tried their best since 1896 to carry out that pledge and to reform the Senate. We have a right to assume that they have striven night and day to devise some way by which they could reform that Senate. Now this government must be intending to carry out those pledges, and in all fairness to them we must assume that they have ever since been endeavouring to find some solution to this problem. They have' been unable to do so. Then in the name of common sense, in the name of everything that is reasonable, is it not time' that a petition was sent to His Gracious Majesty asking him either to remove the Senate, or to reform it in the interest of this country?
Now, some people say there are large matters dealt with in the Senate, and we never know that one of these large matters might come up in regard to which the -Senate might act as a cooling basin, to allow parliament and the country to give further consideration to the matter, in short to act as a check on hasty legislation that might be indulged in by this chamber. Rut look at the province of Ontario-no Senate, no second chamber, no trouble, but dealing with a great many important matters that come right home to the people, matters like direct taxation which the people feel instantly. Now, the province of Ontario has not had a second chamber for years and years, it was abolished almost directly after confederation, and no one ever said that the legislature of Ontario passes hasty legislation, or that the people are not satisfied with it. I believe the only provinces in the Dominion that still technically continue their second chambers are Quebec and Nova Scotia, but so little work have they ever done that scarcely any one realizes that there is a second chamber in those provinces. So I say that in view of -all the important matters that are dealt with by the provincial legislatures with a single chamber, we are justified in concluding that if those legislatures do not need a second chamber neither does this parliament. Why? If it were a matter of sufficient importance, as I have already pointed out, any Bill could be delayed by the home government, and there would not need to be any wrench to the constitution.
There has been another suggestion for reform which the Prime Minister says lie does not approve and that is appointments by the provincial legislatures. I do not think a Senate appointed by the provincial legislatures would work satisfactorily, and I will tell you why. Senators thus appointed would be swayed by purely local influences, they wouid be provincial in their ideas, and partial to the provinces
that appointed them. If any legislation bore rather harder on one province than upon another, you would find the senators from that particular province obstructing that legislation, believing that in so doing they were carrying out the will of the province that appointed them. We would find no independence in a body thus appointed. Let me give you another illustration to show how this so-called independent Senate is a broken reed upon which we cannot rely. Here is a case that might happen any day. The government .might bring down a Bill which was unpopular. Supposing, for instance, that last session the Canadian Senate had seen fit to oppose the government Bill creating a Canadian Navy on the ground that it was unconstitutional. Supposing after the government's majority in this House had voted the Bill through, the Senate had rejected it, and sent that Bill back here. This government has power to appoint senators by its own inherent power, and we all know that whatever government is in power their tendency is to appoint senators of that particular stripe. Does any one suppose that that institution, appointed by the party in power for purely political reasons, is going to resist their masters who appointed them, and would declare their independence of the government that placed any Bill before them? Where would be your responsible government under such circumstances?
Now, I can well understand that any one who was determined on separation from Great Britain might desire that the Senate should continue to exist. But I could not understand an imperialist holding such an idea, because if a man is an imperialist he feels absolutely safe in the fact that the home government would, in any case where vested interests were interfered with, or injustice was being done, interpose its veto within the two years' prescribed by the constitution. But I could understand that a man having in view separation from Great Britain would not wish to see the Senate abolished, because if the country is going to separate from Great Britain then he would want a second chamber here to keep us right instead of the very thing which the imperialist would desire, a right to appeal to the home government under the circumstances I have mentioned. But any one who does not wish a separation from Great Britain might suppose there was no need of a second chamber.
Now, I wish to put a quotation or two on the ' Hansard ' to show what the newspapers are saying about this matter. Take, for instance, the Toronto ' Star,' a paper that is not looking for opportunities to find fault with the present administration. In fact, I think I can go further and say that

it is a very faithful supporter of the government to-day. On January 4, 1909, the Toronto * Star ' said:-
As the matter now stands the Senate is simply an addition to the patronage of the government.
That is the statement of a paper supporting this government.
Patronage in the Civil Service we have learned to endure through custom, but surely it is unwise to extend the system of patronage to the appointment of those who make the laws of the land. Responsible government means the responsibility of the government to parliament, hut who can speak seriously of the responsibility of a government to a portion of parliament appointed by the government itself?
Exactly, if I may interpolate, this is the very point that I was endeavouring to make to-night of a Bill going to the Senate sent up by a majority of this House, and the Senate rejecting it to help out the government. The ' Star ' goes on:-
The plan laid before the Senate by the Hon. Sir R. W. Scott is good in so far as it proposes to substitute election for appointment. An elected Senate, dealing independently with the measures sent up by the House of Commons, including government measures, might occasionally serve a good purpose. It is doubtful whether such a body could work in harmony with a system which requires that the government of the day shall have a parliamentary majority for the support of its measures, hut if it were found unworkable it would probably be a half-way house on the road to abolition, which to many seems to he the logical solution of the problem.
I may not toe in very good company with the ' Star ' tout I call it as a witness. We find the ' Star ' supporting this government strenuously since it came into power. I do not know whether this paper was in existence before the government came into power, but I see that it has been thriving very well since the government has been in power. It says that practical abolition is the logical solution, tout that until you get abolition you had better have an elected body, a half way house to the final consummation so devoutly wished for. The ' Star ' on November 16, 1909, said this:-[DOT]
Against the Senate we wish to register several objections. The least of these is that it is a feeble echo of the party in power in the Commons. When the Senate docs nothing but ratify the will of the Commons, we see it at its best, for we are then having representative government. The will of the elected parliament is not being frustrated by another body, whose memibens are chosen for reasons the people know nothing about, and which no amount of study can enable them to understand. At such a time the Senate is only unnecessary, and nothing worse.
Yet we must qualify the statement, for in Mr. LANCASTER.
that case it is even worse than unnecessary and worse than being a profitless expense, because no member of parliament knows just how soon a vacancy in the Senate may occur, and it is not uncommon to find representatives of the people forfeiting their popularity at the polls confident of reaching that upper chamber where no poll is long enough to reach them.
At another time the Senate is not the feeble echo of the Commons. We submit that it is seen at its worst when it resists the will of the Commons, or undertakes to originate legislation. In that case it weakens popular government, impedes, and frustates it. Why should the people support an appointed House to resist and baffle the purposes of an elected one?
Then I will refer once more to the ' Star,' bringing it down to November 30, 1909. At the end of a long article, all of which I need not trouble the House by reading, we find this conclusion:-
But the fact that the Canadian Senate does not go to such lengths as the British House of Lords does not make it a desirable part of ; our constitution. If birth ought not to make a legislator, neither should a legislator he appointed by the government, which ought to be checked and controlled by the legislative body. It is the tendency of all bodies not elected by the people to become reactionary. The Senate of the United States is in this respect not much better than the British House of Lords. All appointed bodies, freed from the wholesome influence of public control, tend to lose touch with the people, and to voice the opinions and sentiments of privileged classes.
I will give a quotation in rather terse language from a paper for which, if I may be pardoned for saying so, I have more respect, and that is the Toronto ' Mail and Empire."' The Toronto ' Mail and Empire,' writing about this matter on the 5th January, 1910, said this:-
Canadians are being incited by several papers to indignation against the House of Lords as a political institution. Like other human works, the House of Lords is full of imperfections, hut candour compels us to admit that it is both an abler and a more conscientious legislative body than the Senate of Canada or the Senate of the United States. In practice, also, it is more democratic than either of these chambers.
Then, a very short quotation from the Goderich ' Signal,' and a comment from the Hamilton 'Spectator' upon it:-
The Goderich ' Signal ' shouts ' No quarter for the Canadian Senate,' hut would'nt ' no quarters ' be a quicker way of getting rid of that body?
These are terse, and, it may he, somewhat flippant comments upon the Senate, but you may see what they illustrate. Here is the Goderich ' Signal ' saying that there should be * no quarter for the Canadian Senate.' It means that the Senate is abso-

lutely no use in the opinion of the Goderich ' Signal.' Then the Hamilton ' Spectator ' quotes that on January 24, 1910, and says- and I agree with the ' Spectator-that ' no quarters ' would be a quicker way of getting rid of that body; that is to say, furnish no place for them to meet, do not summon them to attend, and let them have their appointments for life. What the ' Spectator ' means is to leave them so that they do not meddle with the popular chamber by interfering with legislation and by obstructing the progress of the country as they are apt to do and have done in the past. The ' Spectator ' means to say: Do not summon them to Ottawa, do not place before them something to enable them to make pretense that they are legislating; let them live out their lives; let them live as long as they possibly can. We hope that they may live for ever, and I do not think that the country would abject to continuing their indemnity but let them not meddle and let them work themselves out, so that, without waiting very long for it, we would have the consummation that is here desired and there would be no more trouble about it. The Toronto ' Globe,' with all its loyal support of this government, says this about the Senate, writing on January 10, 1911:-
It is to be hoped there is no basis of truth for the statement in the opposition press that the total membership of the Senate is to be 'largely' increased. The Senate is too large already. Reform in the direction of abolishing life senatorships and reducing the membership is long overdue.
There are many such suggestions in favour of the abolition of the Senate. Going through newspapers of different kinds and on different sides of politics you find many arguments and these arguments are well known to the Prime Minister, to the cabinet and to those who could, with the force they have behind them, and even without forcing their views through, but by argument and reasoning, find some solution if there is any solution to be found with regard to the Senate. They could find some means of reforming it. But, the time having gone by for any suggested reformation, I have come to the conclusion that the only successful and practical thing to do is to appeal to His Most Gracious Majesty the King to grant us some means for the abolition of it. Before concluding I ought to put on record some citations from a book which I have had the opportunity of perusing since I spoke upon this question last yean This is a new work upon the subject published last year in England, written by Prof. Harold W. V. Temperley, in London, and entitled ' Senates and upper chambers ':-
I read this book with a good deal of care and I think it my duty to put on record
certain of the opinions it contains, written by a British subject and a friendly critic of Canada. At page 43 the author says:
Practical experience of the difficulty of constituting upper chambers in the Australasian colonies even induced Earl Grey himself to modify his bicameral views (?). He declared their danger to lie in the fact that the division of the legislature into two branches withdrew some of the most able and intelligent men from the lower chamber ' in a community not numerous enough to furnish more than a few persons qualified for such duties.' Even if it did not do this the upper chamber might be composed of mere party men without ability, in which case it must become discredited and weak. He was therefore led into a practical advocacy of single chambers for the colonies (8).
I now consider it to be very doubtful, at least, whether the single legislature (chamber) ought not under any circumstances to be preferred.
This is written in 1910. I quote from page 46:
Since the granting of responsible government the Canadian colonies have never shown much enthusiasm for their upper chambers, which have been abolished in four of the provinces. In the beginning the Australasian colonies adopted two chambers with unanimity, but subsequent experience qualified their enthusiasm. In our third group, the South African colonies, the attachment to the bicameral system has, from the first, been singularly lukewarm. Cape Colony adopted two chambers in the early fifties, and appears to have retained them without much protest after the introduction of responsible government (1872). But the Cape upper chamber, being elective, threatened to challenge the supremacy of the lower house. Its example and claims were not encouraging, and they seem to have impressed the other colonies in South Africa. When Natal petitioned for responsible government she made a determined effort to get rid of an upper chamber altogether, and only yielded to the strong opinion of the Home government in the matter (1893). It is quite clear that the upper chambers in the Transvaal and Orange River colony are only temporary ones in their present character, and it is by no means certain that it was not intended that they should be abolished altogether in the future. As for the federal Senate of South Africa the constitution gives it no special protection after ten years; and ' furthermore (this is an open secret) there was a strong party in the convention in favour of doing without it altogether.' The feeling here shown is more significant than any of the other instances adduced. Whatever may have been thought of single-chamber government in a unitary state, it had always been previously considered that an upper chamber was indispensable for a federal state. If the collective wisdom of South Africa could for a moment seriously contemplate doing without one in the federal constitution, it is quite evident that it absolutely condemns the bicameral system for unitary states, and in this judgment we see the severest criticism that the two-chamber system has hitherto received.

But in any case the general testimony of our other colonies to the worth of the bicameral system must he regarded as a somewhat ungracious one. Nowhere is the upper chamber really imposing in the unitary colonies, in few is it actually powerful, in many it is regarded as a rather tedious relic of a by-gone age. In Canada and South Africa, certainly, it is looked upon as an ancestral relative, whose death would not cause any particular grief to the colonies in question, though they do not care to terminate his existence by speedier means. The Home government stands by acting the part of the family doctor, bidding the eager heirs to have patience, and meanwhile doing its best to keep the aged patient alive by cordials and by encouragement.
Again at page 141 this learned author says:
Whatever the theory, which gave birth to the bicameral system, the working out of that theory has been almost directly contrary to the ideals of its founders. The old idea certainly was that the Upper Chamber should be a ' checking ' Chamber, and should in certain cases possess an absolute veto on the will of the people. The progress of democracy has transformed all that, and this idea now prevails only in the state legislatures of America. There it must indeed be admitted that the Upper Chamber may still be a real checking Chamber, but it is only powerful because democracy has rivetted fetters in itself. The election of state senators and popular representatives on the same tenure, the presence of corruption in the Upper Chamber and of lethargy among the electors has tended in practice to a maintenance of old conditions of which nobody in America really approves. But wherever democracy is progressive, wherever the people become more united and better educated, there the idea of a checking Chamber disappears.
Again at page 224 the author says:
In theory, the Senate of Canada possesses equal powers of legislation with those of the Lower House, except that it cannot originate money Bills. It has, however, full power either to amend or to reject them. In practice, its nominee Senate has not proved very important or effective, largely because it has always been the tool of a party. By 1873 it had been filled with the nominees of the Conservative party, and since then it has been refilled according to the views of the party installed in office. A Liberal member was once appointed by the Conservative premier, Sir John Macdonald, but the present Liberal premier, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, has never departed from the strict party rule. Since it is so obviously the creature of party, such a body cannot evidently have much claim on the reverence of the country. The fact that its members are appointed for life might tend to produce some difficulty when the opposing party gets into office, but the balance is gradually redressed as vacancies appear. None the less, if the present Liberal party had only had a short spell of office, their legislation might have been interfered with. In 1873, when the Liberal party was in power for two years, the Conservative Senate vetoed Mr. LANCASTER.
several measures and provoked considerable complaint at the time from the ministry, though McKenzie subsequently acknowledged that the Senate had used its power to suspend rash and hasty legislation, rather than to check genuinely popular or national measures. Since then their opposition has been more guarded, but a popular agitation against the Senate has been growing, and a desire for its abolition is frequently expressed. No methods of adjustment between the two chambers, other than those by conference or committee, have yet been used. By the constitution, however, it is provided that 'if at any time, on the recommendation of the Governor in Council, the King thinks fit to direct that three or six members be added to the Senate, the Governor in Council may, by summons to three or six qualified persons, as the case may be, representing the three divisions of Canada, add to the Senate accordingly/ In other words, a limited creation of life members for the purpose of 'swamping' can be made. A 'swamping' procedure, when exercised, has everywhere tended to reduce the nominee Senate to impotence, and in Canada this actual result has been attained without this stretch of prerogative. It is difficult to resist Goldwin Smith's conclusion that the Canadian Senate is as nearly a cipher as it is possible for an assembly legally invested with large powers to be. At any rate, the prestige attaching to its federal character has been unable to save the Canadian Senate from that curse of impotence and sterility which seems to settle over all nominee upper chambers in purely unitary states.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I am about to conclude; in view of these opinions expressed by a not unfriendly critic writing last year in London, England, and in view again of the fact that for 14 years this government has made no effort to reform what has been an unsatisfactory state of affairs with regard to the Senate of this country, I have the temerity to move an humble address to His Majestv in the form of the motion placed in your hands.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to offer a few remarks on the question before the House, but I am not vain enough to think that I can suggest a remedy for the condition of things which the hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) has placed before us. In his address the hon. gentleman stated that the Prime Minister was unable to find a scheme for the reform of the Senate which met with his approval, out of the many that had been proposed. If I should have the good fortune to offer a means of reform that will meet with the approval of the right hon. gentleman then I shall have spoken to some purpose; at all events I shall make the attempt. I must say that among business men, thoughtful men who are anxious for the progress and development of this country, I have not found any strong sentiment in favour of the total abolition of the Senate. The constitutional difficulties in the way of such a proposal are of

course great. The question of how far a second chamber can steady legislation and can shape it in a proper course to the advantage of the country, is a large one. I think, Sir, that for the purpose of this discussion we must assume that the Senate will continue and that therefore we may direct our attention to some practical plan of reform which will bring the second chamber more in touch with our people and allot to it a more active participation in our legislation. I believe that I voice the opinion of this House when I say that it is desirable that both legislative bodies be kept well in front with the march of thought in the country, and should fairly express and give effect to the best views of the people of Canada. It may be said as an abjection to a second chamber that it may at some period be composed entirely of members of one political school of thought. We on this side of the House trust that that will not happen; but our best hopes may be blasted, and we may see the Senate composed of gentlemen only in sympathy with the dominant party. I believe it is a theory that when a gentleman enters the second chamber he leaves partisanship aside; but I can scarcely hope, from my limited knowledge of those gentlemen, that that will ever be realized. I will even say that should the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. George Taylor) be appointed to the Senate, as we all trust he will be in due time, I doubt if he would wholly forget the battles he fought in the country and in this House, and would not occasionally, when the party spirit ran high, be out for a little blood. It may be, as the hon. member for Lincoln . has said, that the fact that the senators are appointed for life makes them indifferent to the questions which affect the people who are out in the struggle. I believe that is the case.
Summing up the various objections to the Senate, perhaps the strongest that can be urged against it is the life appointment. Old age and bodily weakness comes to all of us; but I think it strikes the average man that there is something peculiarly grotesque in a body of men perhaps one-fourth or more of whom are wholly unfit to discharge legislative duties. It is a condition that I believe the country would rather not have. Understand, I am saying nothing by way of disrespect of the very able gentlemen who form the Senate. However, it is hardly in line with our democratic thought that there should be placemen, men appointed to draw emoluments when they have become unable to discharge the duties of the positions to which they are appointed. I believe that is after all the strongest objection that exists in the minds of public men. If a plan could be devised that would bring the Senate into more activity, that would
secure the appointment of men, not because they have been unsuccessful politicians or because they have contested constituencies and lost, or because they have helped the party in its hour of need, but because they possessed special knowledge of some of the great problems that confront this Canada of ours, we would have a better Senate. We have great problems. Our public affairs become more complex every year. I remember when the tariff question was simply a question of high tariff or low tariff, of 174 per cent or 28 per cent. Now we have every possible shade of tariff-the minimum, the maximum, the preferential, and the favoured nation, and all that sort of thing. A member of this House may come here honestly desirous of studying tariff questions so that he can speak intelligently upon them, and he will spend one or two sessions bqfore he gets the technical knowledge necessary. The same is true of the transportation question, the question of the conservation of our natural resources, and even the greater question of how we shall secure the proper diffusion of wealth and opportunity among all our people and the proper development of our country. All these questions call for men of big brain and big heart, and we ought to have them in one or the other of the governing bodies of this country. In saying this I am not reflecting on the ability of the members of this House; but I make the appeal to hon. gentlemen if it is not possible that men with a larger outlook, a greater viewpoint, could be added to the debating and legislative ability of the Senate. I assume that the average legislative life of a member of the Senate is eighteen years; I think it will be fully that, though I have not made the exact computation. If gentlemen were appointed to the Senate for six years instead of for life, there would be three appointments where there is now one. Six years is a fairly long term, and it would be a -sufficient reward to a gentleman appointed for party services. That would give three times the number of appointments. I am dismissing from this discussion the question of electing senators by the provincial legislatures. The recent, events in the election of senators in the United States have been, I am sure, an object lesson which should satisfy the people of this country for all time to come. I also dismiss the plan of electing senators by large districts. The. burden of discussion and the expense necessary for such elections make that plan unworkable, and under it we would not perhaps secure any better men. The only plan, then, that can be considered is the present one, of appointment, with the change I propose of having three appointments where now there is one. The first appointment might be made, as it has been in the past, by the ministry of the day to reward a faithful supporter

who has done good work in this House and in the country; but to preserve somewhat the balance of power, to prevent the Senate becoming wholly partisan, and to enable the minority to become represented, the next appointment might be made by the hon. leader of the opposition. That makes two of the three appointments. The third appointment then is in the hands of the Prime Minister. Would it be possible that there could be an understanding, a convention or unwritten agreement between the parties, and the great papers representing the parties should agree, that in making the third appointment the Prime Minister should select men who are bulking large in the public service of the country, prominent bankers, prominent newspaper writers, or teachers in our great colleges or railway managers. This country has produced a great many such men, we are bringing them forward all the time, and I believe that men could be got who have been successful in their careers, who would take such an appointment for the honour, not for the emolument. Such men would be of great service to the country and their appointment would have the efiect of making the Senate a continuing body of men of ability. Then the problems that are troubling us now, and we must always have such problems, could be dealt with' by that body with plenty of time, without partisanship, and in that way we could get the best solution of such questions that could possibly be obtained. There may be some difficulty in working out the plan I have suggested, but I believe that it is worthy of some thought, Such men can be obtained and they would bring to the service of the country the special qualities that are needed.
I have expressed my thought on this matter with some hesitation because I realize how great are the questions with which we have to deal. The only solution that could be accepted would be one that could be "brought without disturbing the constitution and without taking an appeal to the King as is proposed in the resolution of my hon..friend (Mr. Lancaster).

speechtext: Hear, hear.

Mr. Speaker, I am rather surprised that my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) should persist in his resolution as he does. I know that my hon. friend is very persistent in his views, but it seems to me that three times hand running in three different sessions is rather overdoing it. My hon. friend from Lincoln is generally a strong supporter or defender of established rights, but in this case he is trying to upset entirely not only established rights, but a solemn agreement. As I understand it, the Senate of Canada was established at the time of confederation. It was established Mr. McCALL.
largely with a view of protecting as much as possible the interests of the smaller provinces. You know that there is a tendency throughout the world to legislate on the principle that might is right. Therefore, I do not blame the smaller provinces for putting in the agreement of confederation, some clauses by which their rights might be protected. When my hon. friend moves a resolution that this House should appeal to the King in Council or to the imperial parliament to abolish the Senate he apparently does not take into consideration that he could not possibly do that without the consent of these smaller provinces, and of the Senate itself, unless he absolutely overpowers them, and goes over their heads. I am quite sure that even my hon. friend would not ask us to break a solemn pledge even if we have the power. Therefore, the only way that the Senate can be either abolished or reformed, so tar as I can understand, is to get the consent of the Senate itself and of all the provinces before we do anything in the matter, unless we adopt the theory that might is right and override them by appealing to the Crown. The smaller provinces, as I understand it, will insist on the protection that has been provided in the constitution of our country, in the Act of Confederation. My hon. friend says that in Ontario they have but a single House. That is quite true. He also says that no wrong or hurried legislation could be passed through this House without being objected to by some members. I quite believe that might be true, but at the same time the majority would govern. I had the honour of replying to my hon. friend on this question once before, and I then said that so far as I knew the Senate or a second chamber was of advantage to this country and was absolutely necessary to prevent hasty legislation. No matter how that second chamber may be established, I still think a second chamber is absolutely necessary to prevent hasty or undigested legislation or legislation that has not been sufficiently considered before being passed. I have no brief to defend the present Senate, but I believe, as I said once before, that if it is going to be appointed just as capable men can be appointed from the ranks of the party in power as from the ranks of the party in opposition. If there was a vacancy in the Senate now, I am free to confess that I think the party in power should have the right to pick out, and that they can select as good men from their own ranks as they possibly could from the ranks of the opposition, and I am perfectly willing that the nomination should be made in that way. I have no particular fault to find with the present Senate. I have been here but a short time, but I know that a number of very useful Bills have been originated in the Senate, and that

some very capable amendments have been made to Bills that went up from this House. These amendments were perfectly right, and no fault was found with them by this House, which adopted them in most cases without discussion. That shows that the Senate are capable. I do not believe that even my hon. friend would venture to say that the individual members of the Senate are not absolutely capable.
I was much taken with the speech of the hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. McCall) because I think he spoke earnestly and spoke his mind. He made some very excellent suggestions. I do not agree that the senators should be- appointed for only six years; if you are going to continue to nominate, I think the term should certainly be longer than that. I think the term should certainly be longer than six years. As to the suggestion of my hon. friend from Lincoln that the Senate should be abolished, I think, with all due deference to the hon. gentleman, that if he really wishes to write his name upon the pages of history he should apply the time and patience he used in preparing speeches in support of Senate abolition to the discovery of means of reforming the Senate if it needs reform. Personally, I do not say that the present form of the Senate should be particularly changed. If that body is to be reformed, it certainly should be, in my judgment, on democratic lines, by election in some form. *My suggestion would be that a certain number of senators be elected at large for each province, or, if not elected at large, that the senatorial districts be larger-per-, haps twice or three times more extensive- than the constituency of a member of the House of Commons.
The hon. gentleman (Mr. Lancaster) says that he introduced a railway measure that was voted for iby 220 members of this House and by 16 members of the Senate, but that 20 members of the Senate threw out that Bill. I remember the Bill lie speaks of, but, unfortunately for me, I was so green that I did not know it was( going through the House until it was passed. Personally, I was opposed to the Bill, and would have voted against it if I had had sense enough to know that- it was going through the House. I do not know that any other members were in the same position, but I know that there were many who were not in favour of the Bill. I would suggest to the hon. gentleman thatj perhaps, the Senate did not do so badly' in that case.	j
What I said was that the House passed the Bill unanimously three times. The hon. gentleman (Mr. Nesbitt) was in his seat and did not* raise his voice against it.

And I have told the hon. gentleman whv. and I am quite frank 86
in my acknowledgment. The hon. gentleman said also something to the effect that those who were in favour of abolishing the Senate were imperialists, or that the imperialists need not be afraid to abolish; the Senate because Great Britain would look after our interests, but that those who were in favour of separation from Great Britain-I think that was the way he put it-would oppose the abolition of the Senate.
I said they might be in favour of it possibly.

I consider that a very wonderful thought on the part of the hon. gentleman. I think it was a great draught on his powers of imagination; I confess that it was too much for me; I could notl follow it. As to the usefulness of the| Senate and our need to have our legisla-1 tion checked, let me once more say that! I am aware that the present Senate hast introduced and sent to this chamber valu-l able legislation and that they have made useful amendments in the Bills sent to them from this House. As to the present; personnel of the Senate, so far as I know, the Senators are as capable, man for man, as members of this House. In one thing I agree with my hon. friend (Mr. Lancaster), and that is that some of the Senators have attained too great an agd to take a useful part in the work of legislation. But it is extremely difficult to fix an age limit, because some men at seventy are better than they were at fifty, some men of seventy-five, with matured minds and wide experience, are better for the work of legislation than other men at sixty-five or less. Therefore. I could not advocate the age limit for the Senate.
I do not think my hon. friend can expect many members of this House to vote for his resolution. Certainly the idea of abolishing the Senate is repugnant to me. I would assist in any way I could a reasonable measure of reform of the Senate, and I believe that the best reform would be by a system of election.

, My hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) has spoken very strongly in favour of the abolition of the Senate. Perhaps, as' a younger man, I would have agreed with him; but I must say that my experience in Ottawa has led me to see that a second chamber is a very useful body. I think that any person who has had experience with our Railway Committee, for instance, would come to the conclusion that he would rather have a measure for which he wished deliberate thought considered in the Senate than in our own House. We know, too, that measures which are very useful indeed are introduced in the Senate, and, after mature consideration,



are brought before this House, and that the work of this House is relieved to a very great degree. The reason why we have not had any considerable agitation concerning the Senate, either for its abolition or reform, lies, I think, in the factj that there has been no conflict between the two Houses.
My hon. friend from Lincoln referred to the resolution which was passed by the Liberal convention of 1893. There had been two events which brought to the mind of the Liberal party, at any rate, the advisability of a change in the Senate. Questions had arisen in the House of Commons involving the rights of minorities. In 1882 a monstrous gerrymander Bill was passed by the government of the day, under which the rights of the Liberal minority were taken away, and if ever there was a time calling for the action of the Senate on behalf of a minority it was then, but that opportunity they ignored. On a later occasion, in 1885, the Conservative government introduced a Franchise Act which was framed with the idea of disfranchising a great portion of the Liberal electorate, and it was only by the strenuous lighting of the very able opposition of that day that the designs of the Conservative government were frustrated. I think it was these two instances in which the Senate had not shown themselves to be the protectors of minorities, that led the Liberal party of that day to declare in favour of Senate reform. There has been no agitation in the Conservative party for a reform of the Senate. I am very glad indeed to be able to congratulate the Conservative party that there is a government in power which has never endeavoured to pass measures in this House which would deprive the Conservative party of their rights, and they have never had occasion to complain of the Senate that that body was not according them full protection. I think in the two instances I have given, you find the reasons why the Liberal party of 1893 were strongly in favour of Senate reform. I have said that the reason there is no agitation to-day is because there is no conflict. It lies further in the fact that this is a democratic body. My hon. friend from North Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) spoke of making the Senate an elective body, that is to say, a democratic body, by giving it co-equal power with this House of Commons. I think, Sir, that would be a mistake. I think it would be a mistake to create another body with co-equal authority from the people with this House of Commons, because to that degree it would diminish the power and authority of the House of Commons. The seeuriry which we have in Canada to-day for sound legislation lies in the fact that the Senate agrees with the House of Commons. For that reason I think it is desirable that the Mr. McCRANEY.
power of appointment should continue to continue to reside in the government of the day.
I agree with my hon. friend from Norfolk (Mr. McCall) in his suggestion that the change be made in the direction of term appointments, and he suggested a period of six years. For myself I would prefer a longer period, but that is a matter of detail which could be settled rarer on. I think there are many reasons why term appointments would be preferable to life appointments as they now exist. My hon. friend from Norfolk referred to one fact that should be borne in mind, namely, that those who go into the Senate and remain there for a long time are not at their best in attending to whatever duties are laid upon them. After their term of appointment has expired the government of the day would be justified in telling them that there were younger men who could take their places. In many instances no doubt that would not be necessary, because their friends would advise them not to seek their seats again. My hon. friend from Norfolk suggested a way in which the Senate should be appointed in future; he suggested that the leader of the opposition should be called into council, and that representatives of the (press should also ibe consulted. Those are matters which I need not enter into, those are things which could be worked out by the Premier himself if he thought such a plan desirable. I do think however that it is altogether, desirable in the interest of this country that the present life term of senators should be abolished for the future. When a new government come into power the Senate would be brought into correspondence with this chamber in a short time by the method of term appointments. This suggestion which has been made by my hon. friend from Norfolk has exceptional merit in the fact that it is one which would secure, not only the approval of this House, but of the Senate itself. There are many schemes proposed, some of which are impracticable and fanciful, and very few of which would carry in this House. There are a number on both sides of the House who look forward to a seat in the Senate at some time in the future. Fortunately in this country we have government by the government, and I think if the. government took hold of this question and asked this House to carry through such a measure, ensuring the present senators the tenure of their seats during their lifetime, there would. he no difficulty in passing such a measure in both the House of Commons arid the Senate. Some might say that the suggestion does not go far enough. I say let us go that far at least. I 'hope the government 'will bring in a Bill to carry out the suggestion made by my hon. friend from. Norfolk.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
This is the third time and the third year that my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) has introduced a resolution to abolish the Senate. This is the third time that he has endeavoured to convince the House that it would be advisable, in the public interest, that we should depart from the principle laid down in the constitutional Act, and lay aside altogether one of the pillars of the state, which were erected by those whom he properly describes as the fathers of confederation. The persistency of my hon. friend in face of adverse results shows that his motives are sincere, and the earnestness with which he has pursued his design commands our respect. At the same time, I may be permitted to observe to my hon. friend that he has approached this question, not from the point of view of any principle, but on the ground that the Senate as at present constituted has not reached that standard of excellence which we had a right to expect from it. That is a view which may be controverted, but I do not here and now enter into any controversy with him upon the point. The question which he has presented to the House and the manner in which he has presented it resolve themselves simplv into this proposition: Is it, or is it not, advisable that the whole legislative authority and power of the country should be reposed in one single chamber, as he suggests; or rather shall continue to be divided under the bicameral system which we have had since confederation? If, in answer-to that question, we look to the experience of the world at large, there can be hut one conclusion, and that conclusion must be adverse to the policy laid down by my hon. friend. I believe that in this he will agree with me-I speak under correction-but I think that what I am going to say is absolutely correct, that I do not know of any country at the present time blessed with sovereign and constitutional power in which is not to be found the bicameral system. I do not know of any civilized country at this moment where they have the legislative powers concentrated in one single body. So far as my information goes, and I think my information is absolutely correct, there is no country that I can think of, at all events, in which they have not the legislative power divided between two bodies. Let me go further, and ask my hon. friend what he understands to be at present the issue in England. Not, perhaps, in the absolute form in which my hon. friend has presented it, but at all events the <iu.pstion is not at present one between two different sets of views-that is to say, the retention or total abolition of the second chamber. I am not avrarp, nor do I believe that at this moment the total abolition of the second chamber, as the hon. gentleman 86*
proposes, is the issue, but what has been proposed is that they shall so check the veto power of the second chamber as to make it of no use and to put an end to it. That is the proposition which is now before the British people, and unless I mistake my hon. friend altogether, I believe that if he were an English elector he would not propose that Great Britain should put an end to the second chamber,

I certainly would not. I understand the distinction. There they have no other cooling basin than the House of Lords. Here w^e have the Imperial parliament, to which we can appeal, and w'e do not need a Senate.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
I understand my hon. friend then to say that it is advisable that the legislative power should have a check. He is not proposing that we should have a legislative body altogether without any check. I agree with him in that. So far as we can see it would not be wise that we should have a legislative body absolutely without any check at all. But, he thinks we have a check in this country under our constitution by the power of disallowance. May I be permitted to suggest to my hon. friend that the remedy which he proposes would be far worse than no check at all. The remedy which he proposes of disallowance, if it were exercised at all, would lead to confusion, and even worse than confusion, and to very serious results indeed. I doubt very much that, if the power of disallowance which is now, under our constitution, vested in the British parliament, had been exercised in the way which my hon. friend suggests, the relations between the mother country and this country would have been as cordial as they are at the present time. We in this government also have the power of disallowance over the province of Ontario where they do not have a second chamber. Is my hon. friend prepared to take the stand that he would advise, as a check upon the province of Ontario, disallowance by this government of the legislation of the province of Ontario? Why, Sir, if we were to apply that remedy, which my hon. friend says ought to be applied to Canada by Great Britain, if we were, to apply that check over the legislature of Ontario, my hon. friend would be the first man to protest against the superior power of this government being exercised to set aside the will of the people of Ontario as expressed in their legislature. A few years ago the legislature of Ontario passed an Act which, in my judgment, was very unsound legislation, in the judgment of many others not only on this side but, I believe, on the other side of the House was very unsound legislation. My hon. friend the Minister of Justice (Sir Allen Aylesworth) when

urged to disallow such legislation, would not do so. Why? Because he agreed with the legislation? Far from it; he disagreed with it altogether. He stated that it was a most infamous Act, that it was a direct violation of the rights of private owner-shin, but he said: I will not advise this government to exercise the power' with which they are vested under the constitution to substitute our own wisdom for the will of the people of Ontario as expressed by their legislature. .He went further and said that if it pleases the people of Ontario in their legislature to confiscate private property, if they are prepared to do so by their legislation, the remedv is in the people of Ontario, and not in this government. If the Minister of Justice had advised the government to take the course which my hon. friend has suggested in his speech and to disallow that legislation of the province of Ontario I am much mistaken if my hon. friend the member for Lincoln would not have been one of the first, if not the very first, to rise and protest against the tyranny of the government in thus interfering with the sovereign power of one of the provinces constituting this confederation. Let me apply this same reasoning to the will of the people of Canada as expressed in this House. Suppose we pass a Bill in this House by a narrow majority, if you will, or by a large majority, one of those Bills upon some of those questions which in this country unfortunately at times have aroused a great deal of popular passion and prejudice, and if there were no Senate to check the legislation of this House, and the imperial government were to try to disallow this legislation and substitute their own view of what was right for our own view of what was right, does my hon. friend believe that this would be. conducive to the good-will which we expect to endure for ever between the people of Canada and the people of Great Britain? If my hon. friend wanted to plant seeds of discord, and to bring about the dissolution of the ties which bind us to Great Britain, the remedy which he suggests would be the very remedy that would produce that result.
Will the right hon. gentleman tell me the reason for placing that section in the constitution? It is not there for waste paper.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
It is not there for waste paper, but I do not believe it has been placed there for any such purpose as my hon. friend has suggested. It was not placed there in order to review our legislation, but simply for extreme cases where this parliament might do something which, in the view of Great Britain, w'ould be injurious to the relations existing between Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
this country and Great Britain. We have
exercised our power only occasionally. Since we have been in office we have never disallowed any legislation except that which we thought interfered with the policy of this government, and the interests of the empire at large. The only legislation which we have disallowed, except in some instances where some legislature had clearly gone beyond the sphere of its jurisdiction, has been the immigration legislation of British Columbia. We did that, because we thought that the legislation of British Columbia in respect to Japanese immigrants would entangle us in difficulties from an imperial point of view. That was the only reason why we did it, and it is for some such purpose that the Sovereign power of Great Britain has been maintained in the constitution. But, Sir, was it ever contemplated by Sir John Macdonald,, or Sir George Brown or any of the fathers of confederation, that the parliament of Great Britain should have the rignt in matters of legislation to substitute their wisdom for ours and that they should be able to say: The parliament of Canada has 'passed legislation on this or that subject which we think to be wrong, and therefore, we shall disallow it. If anything of that kind were attempted long e'er this there would have been strong protest. However, the government of Great Britain have never attempted anything of the kind except on one or two occasions, when the disallowance of our legislation was immediately followed by strong protest from the government and the people of Canada. If my hon. friend (Mr. Lancaster), who I am sure is in earnest in this matter will consider it carefully, I believe he will come to the conclusion that what he proposes would not only be no remedy at all, but that it would prove an element of discord in the happy relations which now exist between us and Great Britain. If there is one thing more certain than another it is that when we obtained responsible government it was with the view that the legislature of this country should be responsible to the people of this country and to nobody else. It was never intended that with respect to the subjects which were entrusted to us by the Act of confederation the Canadian parliament should be responsible to the people of Great Britain and not to the people of Canada. Any departure from that principle would be a thing to be deprecated. Now, Sir, if the considerations which I have presented to my hon. friend be correct, he will I think agree with me that his remedy cannot be accepted. If we must have a check over the legislation passed by the House of Commons, this check is not to be found in Great Britain, but within the purview of our constitution, and consequently in a second chamber. I am rather sorry that the hon. gentleman (Mr. JANUARY 30, 1911
Lancaster) instead of moving such a drastic resolution, did not follow the example of my hon. friend from Norfolk (Mr. McCall), and give us the benefit of some suggestions as to reform of the Senate. I think we are all, on both sides of the House agreed, at the present time, that the constitution of the Senate is susceptible of amendment. Nobody pretends that it is not. But, there was a time when the views of gentlemen supporting the Conservative party were not so decided on the question as they appear to be at this moment. There was a time when they thought the Senate was perfect. Not long after the present government came into office, I remember that Sir Charles Tupper sitting opposite _me said:	Thank
God we have a Senate. That was the occasion when the Senate rejected our proposed railway to the Yukon, and which had it been adopted would I believe have been one of the most useful pieces of legislation ever put on the statute-books.
And on that occasion, many of your own friends, if not yourself, also thanked God there was a Senate.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It certainly was not on that occasion.
Yes it was.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: On that occasion it was Sir Charles Tupper who thanked God there was a Senate.

There was a very good story and fairly well authenticated which said, that a very good friend of the Prime Minister, on the night of the passage of that Bill through the commons or on the eve of the vote which was to take place in the Senate went home and it is said spent many hours at his bedside praying God to put into the minds of the senators the will to defeat that iniquitous Bill which he himself had voted for in the Commons.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
That is a legend, and cannot have foundation in fact. If ever there was a mistake committed by the Senate of Canada it was when they rejected that Bill, which had it been passed would have afforded Canada access to the Yukon which we have not now except by passing through American territory. In all earnestness I repeat, that if ever there was a mistake committed by the Canadian Senate it was on that occasion. And what did they reject the Bill for? They rejected it because it was supposed at that time that the Yukon was covered with gold, and that we were paying an enormous price for the railway ; whereas it h-as turned out that had the bargain been made the railway would have been built on the best terms obtainable, and better terms than ever again will be obtained. Had my hon. friend (Mr. Lancaster) suggested some plan to reform the Senate I would have thanked
him. The hon. gentleman told us that in 1896 he was in favour of the Senate, but that he has Changed his mind. Well, he is not the only man on the opposite side of the House who has changed his mind, because many of these gentlemen opposite who were against the reform of the Senate before 1896 are in favour of that idea now.
