However, the difficulty has always been to discover a proper method of reform. It is a question which is open to argument, and speaking for myself personally I am open to conviction upon this point. I am ready to receive any valuable, practical suggestion which may come from either side of the House, but we must all admit that for the last 14 years we have not received any suggestion, which in our opinion leads to a proper reform of the Senate. And, what should be a proper reform of the Senate. First of all, objection was taken to life appointment, and there is a good deal in that objection. For my part, I would rather favour an appointment for a limited time, not six year3 as was suggested by my hon. friend from Norfolk, because I think that term would be altogether too short, but for 12 or 15 years. That would suit me, and if any such suggestion were made I would be ready to consider it. Now, by whom should the appointments to the Senate be made ; should they be nominative or elective? So far as I can see there is no one within the reach of my voice who would favour an elective Senate. We think we have elections enough at the present time, and I have not heard any one to suggest that the senators should be elected by the people. That being so what is the next plan? It has been suggested that the senators should be elected by the local legislatures, and I am free to confess that in my earlier days when my hair was not so white as now, I would have favoured that reform myself. It must be admitted that in the early years of the American republic the Senate of the United States reached a point of excellence which has hardly ever been surpassed in any other country in the world. But, it must be admitted that of late years especially, the appointment of senators by the different states has not worked so satisfactorily as it did in the earlier years of the republic. I would not be prepared to say for all that, that I would be against the appointment by the local legislatures although my enthusiasm in that respect is not as great as it was in my younger days. But, if it were proposed to elect a certain proportion of the Senate by the local legislatures and that we should retain the appointment of another portion in our own hands, perhaps we might find there a proper measure of reform. At all events, the one thing to be kept in mind in any reform of the Senate is, that the different sections of public opinion should be represented on the floor

of the Senate. It may be said, and I have heard it said : Why does not the government itself select senators from the different political parties. Well, I have only to say that the government is composed of men who are very human, and I do not know that whether the appointments were, made by a Conservative or a Liberal government they differed very much in degree as to the mode of selection. It will, of course, always be very difficult to have the different classes of the community properly represented if the nominating power is not centered in one body, but in different 'bodies. We would have that if a part of the electors of the Senate were to be appointed by the local legislatures or some such body. In saying this I am not expressing convictions which are deliberate and final ; but I say that these are all matters for consideration. My hon. friend from Lincoln seemed to be strongly in favour of that 'point of view ; and when he favours us next year with the same subject, he may possibly present us with a scheme of reform, rather than a proposal for the total abolition of the Senate. As my hon. friend knows in advance what will be the result if he presses his motion now, and as he -has elicited the opinion of the House, perhaps he will agree to withdraw it. If not, we shall have to divide the House upon it.

Mr. Speaker, as I understand, there is to be a vote taken on this question. I give that as my reason for making a few observations upon it. Ever since my entrance into this chamber I have watched somewhat closely the history of our own Senate, and have read something of the history of second chambers in other countries. From time to time there has been agitation amongst the electors, in my riding as well as in others, for the abolition of the Senate-by some on the ground that it was too expensive, by others on the ground that it was unnecessary to have a chamber corrective of the House of Commons, and by others upon the ground that the senators, instead of acting as non-partisan, have been in the habit of acting as partisans, and that this would be found to be the case no matter which political party was in power. Therefore, taking an interest in the question, I have watched the career and history of the Senate very closely, and have also read the history of second chambers in other countries, and I agree with the right hon. the Prime Minister that there is no civilized country that I am aware of which has constitutional government that has not a second chamber. If we are to learn from history and experience-and I respectfully submit that these are the most reliable educative sources that we can possibly have-there is only Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
one conclusion with regard to this question that we can reach, that is, ttigl it would not be wise to be without a second chamber. I think that applies just as strongly to Canada, where we profess to have typical constitutional government, as it does to England, the mother of parliaments, or to Germany, or to the United States, or to other countries.	_
The hon. member 'for Lincoln said that at confederation, when we established the second chamber, the conditions were different from what they are now, and the people did not know as much about government and governments, and that was the reason we had a second chamber. Well. I do not think so. At that time men were elected to the Senate just as members of the House of Commons are elected to-day, only they represented larger constituencies. In my own district, one of the first ejections I ever took part in was that in which one of the candidates for the Senate, Sir David L. Macpherson, ran for the Brock and Saugeen division, which included three counties. But what did we find? For the county of Grey there were three members in this House, for the county of Bruce three members, and for the county of Sim-coe two or three members. Yet we found that the senator who represented the larger district composed of these three counties was deliberately antagonized in legislation by the members ele-cted to the Commons for the same counties by the same class of people. It seemed to me that that was not a healthy system, and I think so still. While it might be admissible to elect a limited number to the Senate, I do not think it is a sound principle to have the same electorate elect men to the Senate and also to the Commons, and have them antagonizing each other just as the two political parties do in this House. Then it occurred to me that a limited number of senators ought to be appointed by the provincial legislatures, and I still hold to that idea. Perhaps I was influenced in it by the system that prevails in the United States. I agree with the right hon. the First Minister that in the early history of the United States it was generally conceded that the Senate was a very useful and important body, but it seems to me, as it does to a great many others in this country, that their system has rather degenerated of late years, and might, in the interest of the country, be reformed in some direction as well as our own.
Now, the first question we should settle in our own minds is this: Is or is not a second chamber desirable? I think most readers of the history of constitutional government in other countries will agree with me that it is desirable. If that be so, what should we do if ours is not fulfilling the indications of what a second chamber

should be? We should apply ourselves to the task of bringing that chamber into harmony with the needs of constitutional government. Do we pretend to say it is an impossible task? The man who admits that acknowledges weakness on his part, no man should lie down and say that anything is impossible that can be accomplished in any other part of the world. Most things that at first sight look to us impossible have been solved in different ages of the world by intelligent men who have sincerely .and honestly applied themselves to the task with continuity of purpose, with patience, pluck and perseverance. If we thus apply ourselves to the task of reforming the Senate, that problem will be solved. The present government promised reform, there is no doubt about that, they do not deny it.
How far have they got in 14 years?

They have not succeeded and even if they stayed here for off years without succeeding that would not-be an argument that others could not accomplish a reform. Many governments have failed in the attempt to do things which their successors have succeeded in doing. We .should apply ourselves to the task of reforming the Senate and bringing it into harmony with the needs of the country rather than abolish it.
The hon. member defends his argument for its abolition by citing the fact that Ontario has only one chamber, and he asks who is dissatisfied with the legislation in Ontario. I say that during the 33 years that the Hon. Sir Oliver Mowat and his friends were in power, had there been a second chamber very much of the pernicious legislation that was put on the statute-books of that province, to its detriment and de-. struction, and to the injury of its people, would not have been in operation to-day.' There is no doubt of it whatever in my mind. Because it is going on smoothly now and seems to fulfil the indications of the situation-

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Hear, hear.
Mr. SPROULE-according to our honest judgment, whether it be right or wrong. That is not saying that we should always have a second chamber, because for a few years, we think they have done right

Mr. MoCRANEY. Does the hon. gentleman think there should be a second chamber now in Ontario?

I am not debating tliat>
because I would have to travel into a wider field, I am only answering the argu-! ment of my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr.i Lancaster) which, to my mind, was very-weak. That hon. gentleman says we have)
a corrective power in the veto, and there is no need of a second chamber. As the First Minister said, what Bills do we veto that come up from the provinces? We veto, with one exception, and even that is not exclusive, such Bills as are passed by provincial parliaments outside or partially outside of'their jurisdiction. That is the only legislation the federal parliament dare veto. Would they dare to veto a provincial Bill wholly within the rights of the province? I do not think so, because if they did, the result would be that they might raise such a storm as would cause almost an insurrection or something equally as bad. It was said that we vetoed the British Columbia Bill regarding immigration. It must be remembered that immigration is one of the subjects with which we have to deal, and although there was another question involved in that subject, outside of the fact that Japan is a friendly ally with England, and we could not afford to shut out the Japanese from Canada as a matter of policy, we could have vetoed that Bill on the ground that this parliament had the right to deal with immigration. It would not be wise to depend on the veto power, for if it were exercised we would very soon be in conflict witlj England, we would soon find cause to blame England for interfering with what we regarded as our proper and legitimate rights. For these reasons I am opposed to this resolution. I have always been in favour of a second chamber, and unless conditions in the future are very different from what has tran-t spired in the past in the parliament of this country I shall continue to hold that* view. I think that one of the defects in1 the second chamber has been that too many appointments have been made from certain classes. For instance, there are a great many men in that chamber connected with banks, with loan companies, with financial corporations, and great institutions of that kind, and some with manufacturing corporations. I have not objected to that with regard to the latter because I do not think their proportion is too numerous. I have said that when we send up Bills containing very proper and wise provisions either to restrain or control these corporations, we never succeed in getting them through the second chamber. Why? Because too many presidents of banks, too many men connected with loan companies, insurance companies or other financial corporations or railway corporations, are in the Senate, and they can always influence the Senate to the extent of preventing our Bills from passing. But that can all be remedied by a proper selection. It is not at all an impossible task, in fact to my mind it would be a very easy task. Therefore we need

not urge that as a reason for the abolition of the Senate.
For these reasons I am prepared to vote against the motion. For friendly reasons, 1 would like to support my hon. friend) from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster), because we agree in nearly everything with which we are associated in parliamentary life, we seem to think very much alike on many lines; but this is one of the things on, which I disagree with him, and I do so because of my honest conviction that the day has not come when this government could or when we should wisely dispense with the second chamber in the parliament of Canada.

The question of second chamber reform is up for discussion in the mother country of Great Britain. It is also up in the adjoining republic of the United States. It is up even here in Canada in a way because the Senate of the parliament of Canada has recently been discussing how it could become a more useful body. I think that a case has been made out here to-night not for the abolition of the Senate, but for its reform. I believe that if something is not done in the way of reform of the Senate there will be a wider agitation in the country for its abolitiop, because to my mind a Senate appointment for life is an anomaly and will not meet with the approval of the people. A Senate that is constituted almost entirely of one party is an anomaly and is contrary to democratic ideas. Therefore, after the confession the Prime Minister has made to-night, I think it is incumbent upon him to deal with this question. And certainly there have been suggested in the House to-night at least two valuable reforms. One is that the life term for senators should cease immediately, or, at least, as soon as we could get sanction for it, probably with the consent of the Senate. And the second is that the senatorial term should be limited,-I would suggest that the limit be six years with, perhaps, eligibility for re-election. I think also that some senators should be elected by the legislatures and some appointed by the government. But the thing is to deal with the matter. We have been promised this for years. The government have assumed the responsibility of supplying the leadership necessary to put into law what seems to be public opinion, and it can hardly be doubted that public opinion is in favour of some kind of reform of the Senate. The Senate has confessed that they themselves would like to see improvement. The second chamber in England is ready for extensive reform, and that question is now being threshed out there. And, in view of the fact that the government will probably propose, within the next year or two a large increase in the Senate by the addition of new members to represent Mr. SPROULF
the West, it is clear that that proposal when made should be accompanied by some proposal for Senate reform. The address of the hon. member for Norfolk (Mr. McCall) I think commended itself to every member of the House. The change he proposes is not a sweeping change but is in the direction of making the Senate more representative, taking away its one-sided character and fitting it to do better work. The Senate say they wish to do more and better work. And the quantity of legislation now presented in parliament is so vast and the subjects considered so numerous that there should be a better division of labour between the two Houses. My contention is that reform of the Senate is long past due, and some kind of reform should come almost immediately, and certainly in connection with the increase in the Senate of which we hear rumours, rumours that, I believe, have good foundation.
As to the suggestion of the hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) that the interests have too large a representation in the Senate, I quite agree with that opinion. When did this democratic government ever propose, for instance, to put a representative of labour in the Senate? In England, there is representation of the labour interests. And I should say that the farming interest is not sufficiently represented in the Senate.	.
And where are our universities?

I do not claim super-excellence for the universities, or that they should be represented over other portions of the community, but the working interest and the farming interests should be better represented in the Senate. In the old days we heard a good deal more about representation of the farmers in the Senate than we do to-day. The only men who seem to be considered as candidates for the Senate are those who have served in this House and those identified with the interests. I do not believe in members of this House going to the upper chamber. Reasons may be given for the occasional exception. Or, perhaps, there might be something in the idea that members who have served in certain capacities in this House should ex officio become members of the Senate. But the wholesale appointment of members of this House to the Senate as now carried on does not tend to promote the independence of this House, and it involves a wrong exercise of political patronage which has often been condemned by hon. members opposite. I have been reading an English review which says that, if the upper chamber is not representative and is not equal quality with the other, a gramophone would do for the other House. And that

is what people will be saying-that a gramophone or a rubber stamp would do for a Senate. But the Senate can be made a useful body. The best men in the country should be in it. They should frame Bills and make necessary investigations. The House of Lords in England is a useful body in that respect, and has, time and again, justified its existence by what it has accomplished in this way. I would like to see a reformed second chamber in Canada, taking a larger share of the work of legislation. And the Prime Minister, as I have said, should take this matter up. He said last year in answer to the arguments that I brought forward:	What would you do?
My answer is: if the Prime Minister is not prepared to assume responsibility, let him make way for those who are. I believe he blocks the way. He says he has a mandate-and so he has-to carry on the government. But he has given a pledge to do this work, for his party pledged themselves to reform the Senate. When is the fruit of that promise to appear? It seems further away than ever.
Perhaps that fig tree is barren.

Perhaps it is. But I will not go so far as to say that, for while there is life there is hope. If the Prime Minister will assume his proper responsibility and propose reform at least in connection with the proposal for an increase of the Senate membership, if that is to come, I think he will have the commendation of the country.

One word by way of explanation; I think I was the first member of this House to introduce a resolution in favour of the abolition of the Senate. If the present resolution comes to a vote, I shall vote with the mover of the resolution, although I do not agree with all the arguments he has advanced. While I introduced such a resolution some years ago, I am quite ready to say to-day that I do not believe there is that popular and widespread demand in the country for the abolition of the Senate that I had supposed existed. The hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) has said that a movement for the abolition of the Senate would carry to-day bv popular vote. It is probable that such would be the pronouncement of the Canadian people, but I believe that would be largely because of the appeal to the public on the ground of dollars and cents, the money cost of maintaining the Senate. I would not like to see the Senate abolished for such a reason; I do not think at all that it would be a sufficient reason for doing awav with the upper chamber. One of the great reasons why I would like to see the upper House done away with would be that there are among the
senators to-day men who are quite capable of representing constituencies in this House and who would be in this House were they not in the Senate. I believe that men of ability and of business and legislative experience would be of more value to the country in the House of Commons than they are or can be in the Senate. Further, I think there is at least a danger that an upper House composed as it must sometimes be under the present system of men^ a very large majority of whom are upon one side of the political line, may prove an obstruction to legislation. A third reason why I would like to see the upper chamber done away with, and that is by all means the least of the three reasons, is the money cost of maintaining the Senate. As to reforming the Senate, it has always seemed to me, and I have paid a great deal of attention to every method of reform, or any suggestion of reform which I have heard advanced by any person, either in this House, or in books that I have read, that no method I have heard suggested, yet seems to me likely to afford any improvement. I believe the Senate as we have it to-day is better than it would be under any system of suggested reform. However, what we have before us now is not a suggestion of reform, but simply a resolution to abolish.

I do not suppose I can throw any bright light on this matter. But as an old parliamentarian, and now for some time in public life, I have my views with reference to the matter. Two things seem apparent in this recurring discussion year after year. One is that my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster), whose spirit of combat always rises as difficulties present themselves, will never be wanting in an incentive for his attacks upon the Senate in the line of abolition. The task will always be there, and my hon. friend will always have an obstacle quite sufficient to call forth all his better powers in his attempt to abolish the Senate. The other fact equally apparent is that it gives a yearly opportunity for the leader of the government to express how open he is to conviction-open at both sides, it seems to me, open for any conviction or any suggestion to come in, and equally open to let it fly out into the air. Now, my right hon. friend commenced with saying that the Senate was one of the great pillars of the state. I agree with him in that respect that the Senate theoretically is one of the great pillars of the state. But these pillars of state may become pretty dilapidated, and. on the other hand so strong in sustaining power as to arouse our admiration and enthusiasm when one contemplates them. As an architect looking from his point of view upon

these great pillars of state, one, two or three of them, as may be, I wonder that the feeling does not grow strong within him to repair the damages occasionally and keep these pillars of state up to at least their former greatness, and if possible to idealize them a little, and make them more worthy of the times. He is urged to do that.
My right hon. friend had some fun with members on this side because of their change of views. A number.of years ago, he informs the House, the Tories had every confidence in the Senate, but at present they seem to have had a change of view. My right hon. friend is open to the same sort of rejoinder. It is not more than fifteen or sixteen years ago that my right hon. friend had very strong views with reference to the Senate. At that time he believed that it ought to be either ended or mended, and he inclined to the idea of immediate emendation. But fourteen years have passed by, and my right hon. friend has yet to make his first motion towards carrying out that pledge of the Liberal party, which was well understood in this country to be a pledge to reform the Senate so as to bring it more into accord with the conditions of the present time.
There is no need of speaking about that matter of the Yukon railway, but it might be as well to remind my right hon. friend that although the scheme was thrown out in the Senate there came a time not long after when my right hon. friend, if he had thought this measure was so necessary to the development of this country ajid the opening up of the Yukon, could have carried that proposition with the Senate in his own favour. But my right hon. friend says now that is too late. Why? Because then it was believed that all the country was filled with gold, afterwards it turned out there was no gold there at all. Surely my right hon. friend would not be guided by a number of men who wanted to build a railway and give him a gold brick. So I do not think my right hon. friend was very happy in that allusion. -
For my own part I am not able, I am sorry to say, to support my hon. friend from Lincoln in his motion for the abolition of the Senate. For the present at least I think a second chamber is here to stay, provided it be fairly constituted. I agree a good deal with my hon. friend from York, who said that unless something is done to make the Senate more effective and to bring it more in accord with the conditions of the time, the sentiment for abolition will grow, and it may grow very speedily. I think it is a pity that that conviction should be allowed to spread amongst the people, and I am not sure but that my right hon. friend is responsible therefore in not carrying out his pledges so far as we can see by one Mr. FOSTER.
single effort to reform the Senate. He has contributed to the adverse feeling that is growing in this country against the continuation of the Senate on the present conditions. Each year that passes the confidence and respect of the public in the Senate does not grow stronger, but on the other hand I think becomes weaker and the problem therefore will become more difficult to solve. I do not believe on the other hand that the patronage system is the proper system upon which to base the second great pillar of state. It is not only absurd but absolutely demoralizing to public life to have the 87 or 88 appointments to the Senate of the country absolutely in the hands of one man, the leader of the government, or of the party for the time being. The principle involved is this, that you simply make the Senate a clearing house for party exigencies, you simply make the Senate an extension of the patronage system. It enables you to say to a recalcitrant member; to the man whom you want to do something for you in political life, or for your party or to any one of these men in a hundred different exigencies that come up: There is a place in the Senate for you, if you do thus and so. Gentlemen like the leader of the present government would not approach a man in that blunt way, but there are methods by which this intimation can be made which are just as effective as if it were made in the language I have just used. But, is it not a tremendous absurdity to put into the hands of one man in the working of the concurrent branch of the legislature that appointive power? It is absurd. It is not only absurd but it is demoralizing from the very root up. It is demoralizing to the most straight and honest hearted politician that comes into the leadership of a party, the temptation is too great to be withstood. A man absolutely bends to it sooner or later and ends up by using it to its greatest possibilities. There never was a period in this country when it was being used to its greatest possibilities more than to-day. But my position is exactly the same whether it be used: by one party in power or by the other. It is an absurd, unconstitutional business to take a great trust like that and to make it simply a piece of machinery and enginery for party warfare, and I do not care by whom or by what party it is being carried on. That it is demoralizing does not need any argument from me.
Well, now', are there no methods 'by which the present condition of things could be altered and made better? What are they? I think that rather than face the question of abolition or otherwise, the drift of opinion in this House is as to what methods may 'be adopted towards bettering the present situation. That was a very good argument, a very fine argument, that the Prime Minister used against our looking

272G
to Great Britain, to the prerogative of the Crown, as a check on the legislation of this House. I cannot agree with my hon. friend from Lincoln (Mr. Lancaster) that it is either desirable or sufficient or that it ever could be practically carried out. Two things are against its being carried out. The self-governing responsible parliament here would not put up with it. Blit there is an equally good reason that the King, or the users of the prerogative, would be very shy indeed in using it, so that on one side or the other it would fail in having its effect. Yet, I believe we ought to have a check, and it seems to me the only check we can have is one constituted for ourselves and by ourselves. But, I do not look upon the Senate as being simply a bodv which is to check and revise legislation, for that is largely clerks' work. It is work which can be done with discrimination or otherwise, but it is not a work which requires the highest powers of men and it is not the only or the best work by any means that a Senate could engage in. They are not only to be a check and a supervision upon hasty legislation coming from this House, but we should look forward to a Senate, and we should have a Senate which should become a vital, concurrent part of the legislative machinery of this country, and be able in many respects to give points to the House of Commons, and to do a work .in the legislative work of the country which the House of Commons cannot do. Are we deteriorating in the House of Commons, or are we not? It is not for me to judge of that, each will have his impressions who has had an experience of a longer or shorter time in this House. But, whether we are deteriorating or not this fact seems to me to be true that we spend an enormous deal of time in the House of Commons doing work which is not the best work that we might do. That arises from the fact that party passion and party spirit are at their strongest in the House of Commons that they consequently impose upon us or they seemed to impose upon us the using of a vast deal of time in what does not result in very much good or very much in the way of actual legislation. Now, my idea is that in the Senate you could have a body out of which would be taken the strongly combative partisan and party spirit, which would cultivate a more reasonable frame of mind, which would breathe an atmosphere which was not surcharged with party rancours and party strifes, which would rise above these more petty things, for in reality they are petty, and trivial, and which could devote its time, in that higher, broader and more reasonable atmosphere, to the weightier matters of legislation, of examination, and to the hundred and one lines upon which legislative initiative and afterwards enactment could be made to run. I think that could be 'brought about. I do not see in the Senate to-day, nor have I seen in any day, the same spirit of partisanship as is developed in this House. Whether they be appointed by Tory or Grit the party passions are cooled in the upper House, and they never go to the extent of the wasting of time, and the bickering that they do in the popular branch in the House of Commons. How are you to get that Senate? I have stated that in so far as I am concerned I would absolutely cut out the appointive power for patronage purposes. It is a vicious principle, it cannot be defended on constitutional grounds, and I would cut that out entirely. How then would you get your Senate? The Prime Minister said that he did not know of any person who believed in an elective Senate. He sits every day in Council alongside of a very noted and distinguished colleague of his who is absolutely in favour of an elective Senate-the right hon. Sir Richard Cartwright, Minister of Trade and Commerce. The idea that something ought to 'be done is fully recognized in the Senate itself, and within the last four years they have had very exhaustive and very instructive discussions as to how the Senate could be made better. This discussion was contributed to by Sir Richard Cartwright, and I am free to say that with many of his views I agree in so far as my experience goes. I am in favour then of cutting out the appointive power for patronage purposes. That does not say that I would cut out the appointive power. entirely. I would keep the appointive power, and in looking around I cannot find any source for the application of that power other than the government of the country for the time being.
But, I would restrict the appointive power by two things:	The number to be
appointed should be small and the basis of appointment should be such as would make the Prime Minister ashamed to make it for considerations of party patronage. Under the conditions he would be bound to the country and bound to his own respect, and honour to make these appointments on the basis which had been assigned. [DOT] 1 would give the government of the country the appointment of twelve or fifteen of the senators, but these appointments should be for distinguished service, not patronage appointments at all. Much has been said to-night about the interests being represented in the upper House. There are interests and interests to be represented. You may have bankers in the upper House, and you may have no acknowledged banking authority or expert. A recognized banking authority and expert known in our own country, and better still known the broad world over and

distinguished in that way, would be an acquisition to the upper House which would give it not only dignity, but would give it working power as well. The agricultural interest, it is said, should be represented. So it should, but the agricultural interest which I would have represented would he that expert knowledge of agriculture which makes a man an acknowledged authority in the country. The same with reference to forestry, the same with reference to the fisheries, the same with reference to science, and the same with reference to our universities.
How about labour?

There are labour men and labour men. If I were the appointing power I would be the last man to appoint one who was always prating about how much of a labour man he was. I would hunt through this country for the most distinguished and ablest representative of labour ideas in their broader and better forms, and I would put him in the upper House as the representative of labour. So in all these great lines, I would make the appointive power restricted by and based upon representation of distinguished services in these great interests. I will tell you one reason why I would do it. Such men cannot get into the legislature and cannot get into the Senate along the general line of election from the primaries up. They would not attempt it in the first place, and in 99 cases out of 100 they would be defeated if they did attempt it. Their whole training and conception of life makes them Tevolt against the processes by which it seems_, almost alone, a man can work his way up into the legislature of modern countries. For that reason they might be all the more useful, but for that reason I would make their accession to our parliament, through appointment. I have in my mind's eye today, and so has my right hon. friend, men in all these great walks of life who would be an honour to the Senate of Canada, and who would be of vital help to us. Every once in a while we want expert help. We need it in this House, and we get it sometimes. But to have men such as I could name, in all these different spheres, in our legislative halls in the upper House, at the command of the country-and they would willingly give their services-would be a great thing for Canada; to my mind it would be an inestimable blessing. As for the rest of the Senate I would make it all absolutely elective. We talk of our trust of the democracy, and that we are democrats ; then let us trust the democracy. The democracy may not always go right, but in 99 cases out of 100 they are as apt to go right as the Prime Minister of Canada; they would not make many more mistakes than Mr. FOSTER.	'
he makes. But in order to elect them I would not go to the legislative assemblies. I would not like to bedevil the legislative assemblies by putting that strife and contention in their midst. They have had a long experience of that in the United States, and human nature is human nature on both sides of the line, and we know in what extremes human nature has shown its bad features in the election of senators in the United States. To-day the revulsion of feeling is absolute against . that method of election; to-day the majority of the states of the union have travelled so far that it is only required to get a few more states in line when they will have their convention, and when they will substitute the election of senators by the people for election by the legislatures. That is a bitter experience which we may very well profit from. It is no use arguing the question why the 'prize of a senatorship thrown into a legislative assembly may lead to demoralization, and to consequences which we would all deplore. I did at one time think that was the best way; I do not now. I would trust the people to do it, and I would have the senators elected by larger constituencies, and I would have it so arranged that there should be proportionate representation. What in the world is the reason why-and taking the two great political parties in this country the whole country is about evenly divided-what in the world is the reason why we should come to the condition that one political party has nearly all the representatives in the Senate. And, if the bad judgment of the people keeps this government in power veTy much longer, and if nature makes its demands in the future as in the past, it will not be very long before under the policy pursued conscientiously-no, but pursued continuously -by the Prime Minister, there will not be a single representative of the Liberal Conservative party in the Senate. That alone, Sir, will disgust people; that alone serves to make the unfairness of the thing so apparent that it takes away Irom the influence of the Senate, and inclines men's minds to a desire to get rid of it if it cannot be reformed. So that, in the scheme for election by methods which are well known and easily tried, I would put into that Senate on the elective basis-representing very large constituencies so as to prevent to the utmost any fear of wrong means being employed, and very large constituencies would counteract that to a large extent-I would put into that Senate always a possible majority in favour of the government in power while at the same time guarding against these great disparities which discourage one-half of our people, and keep from its proper outlet and influence the energies of nearly one-half of our people in the legis-

lative work of the upper House. Just as it would be to my mind a calamity to keep any one great party too long out of power, because it stunts legislation, and at the same time prevents new recuperative power having its full effect in legislation to the benefit of the country, just so it is deplorable that in the upper House you should have the condition of things I have described. We would in this way I think, have a House in which the parties shall be proportionately represented, in a calmer atmosphere, coming up fresh from the people at least every seven or ten years, and I would not make the period more than ten years or less than seven years.
That would give constant rejuvenation to the Senate. In a country where changes take place with enormous rapidity, where conditions at a given time are totally different in many respects from the conditions five years previous, it would bring into touch with those changing conditions and the newer currents of life, the body in the upper House, and make it vital and strong. These are in part my views. They are not original in any respect. I listened with delight to my hon. friend from Norfolk (Mr. McCall), in the short, terse, clear presentation of just sensible 'ideas for this House, and I think they might well be taken into consideration by virtue of their own wisdom and their spirit as well. I do>not want to move an amendment against my hon. friend from Lincoln. I want him to have that vote squarely, to see how many will stand by him here. But if I had the power of moving an amendment, I would move one like this, and I hand it out as a suggestion to my right hon. friend. It is a business arrangement. Here is the upper House talking about methods of improving the Senate, and ministers of .the Crown there say it must be improved or dire consequences will follow-men in perfect unity with my right hon. friend. Out in the country the strongest organs of public opinion on the side of my right hon. friend are almost daily calling for something to be done. Here is one. The * Free Press ' said not long ago:
The recent deaths of Sir George Drummond and Hon. G. B. Baker reduce the Conservative strength in the Senate to twenty members out of eighty-seven.
Since the Liberals came to power, not quite fourteen years ago, fifty Conservative senators have died and have been replaced by Liberal successors.
The Conservative minority, attenuated Though it is, is larger than the Liberal representation in the Senate in 1896, when the Liberals came into office.
There were then only seven Liberal members of the Senate, and of these there were three whose Liberalism was nominal.
The Conservative twenty will doubtless diminish; and if the death rate of the past
few years keeps up, it will not take many years to wipe out the minority.
That would reduce our method of selecting a second chamber to an absurdity, and might result in an attempt to bring about reform.
A second chamber is without doubt a necessity in any country made up as Canada is, of a federation of the provinces; but there are good grounds for thinking that our system of determining and maintaining a second chamber is about the worst known, at least to the Anglo-Saxon world.
I could quote others equally strong from equally strong organs of public opinion representing-the political faith of my right hon. friend; but there is no use in taking up the time. Then, it seems to me that something ought to be done. My right bon. friend acknowledges that something ought to be done. In a letter sent by Mm to the Hon. James Young not long ago, in which he asked that gentleman, who was pressing upon him the necessity of carrying out the pledge that was made so strongly and so definitely by the Liberal party in 1893, to give him his opinion, these are the words used by my right hon. friend:
Would you be kind enough to send me a synopsis of the Senate reform which you think should be adopted?
Two aspects of the question have to be considered.
First, the mode of appointment. Should it be an election directly by the people, or by any other body, or by some other mode of appointment other than the one now existing?
Second, should the appointment be for life or for a term of years?
The whole difficulty rests in these two questions; are they insoluble? They do not appear to me to be so; but the Prime Minister for fourteen years has not attempted to solve them. For about half of that time he was declaring that that was a pledge and that it would be fulfilled, all others have been fulfilled-which might admit of some argument. But for the last seven years he has not gone even that far; he has only said, I am open to conviction, I want suggestions, but I do not see any way. When are we to see a way? My suggestion would be this, that a joint committee be apointed from both Houses of parliament- 12 good men from this House and 12 good from the other and that they be asked to take into consideration the constitution of the Senate, the methods of appointment and the distribution of the work, and, after a thorough examination and consideration, to report to the government and to both Houses their plan. We would get the wisdom of the two Houses after examination of all the different systems, with a knowledge of the conditions of our own country thoroughly canvasse'd. We would then get their reasoned opinion upon the subject. We might not agree with their plan, but there at least would' have a basis on

which we might work. As I say, I do not propose to offer this as an amendment, but I offer it as a suggestion that may be worthy of consideration.

Mr. Speaker, as I understand there is going to be a vote. I would like to state why I intend to support the motion. I believe in the bicameral system, particularly under our constitution. But I believe there was a distinct pledge, made by the Liberal party when it was in opposition, to reform the Senate, but this pledge, like others, has not been carried out. What is the mode of constitution of our second chamber? In two words, it is a reward for party services rendered. That is the mildest expression one can apply to the mode of recruiting the second or revising chamber. Is there any better method of organizing that chamber? I do not intend to discuss the many plans that are spoken of, or that are treated in books, but the worst of all is certainly the one that we have in this country. I do not intend to make any reflection on those who sit in that chamber. But I say that to-day the revising, chamber to check hasty legislation, as we imagine the upper chamber ought to be, is constituted in that way; uniformly it is a reward for party service. The reform promised has not been carried out. If it is not carried out I am inclined to support this motion. My right hon. friend is in the position that history has assigned to a pope who was called upon to abolish a great Teligious order. He set out to reform it, and as history informs us he was told by the members of that order that it should remain as it was or cease to be. For my own part, whatever truth there may be in that story, I believe that the Senate, continued as it is under our institutions, is a useless appendage. It is not properly fulfilling its mission. I do not believe in making it elective; I believe it might be recruited under certain rules and principles which would give it the constitution which is desirable as a second and revising chamber, and since it seems impossible to have recourse to, or carry out, that reform, I am inclined to think the proper course to follow is to support the motion of my hon. friend.

Mr. Speaker, one phase of this subject, has not been dwelt on during this discussion to the extent it deserves. A federal government is always, of necessity, in the nature of a compromise. It is a compromise between, on the one hand, a single large independent state and on the other a large number of small independent states. That compromise is always effected by an agreement. The agreement in this case has been embodied in our constitution, and all the discussion practically which has taken Mr. FOSTER.
place to date, all the various suggestions as to the mode of constitution of the Senate and the mode of appointing to the Senate were undoubtedly discussed in the Quebec conference, and the result so adopted is the basis upon which the constitution of the Senate now rests. Reading the resolutions as reported,, one finds innumerable amendments, innumerable suggestions put to the vote and all rejected after due consideration. Undoubtedly at that time there was one feature in connection with the Senate that probably obtained undue prominence; that was the idea of strengthening the central government. The Senate of the United States was especially constituted as a limitation and restraint upon the presidential powers, and as representative of the sovereignty of the States, and no doubt the condition of conflict which existed in the United States at the time of the framing of our constitution led, to some extent, to the framing of the constitution as relating to the Senate in a way to secure the strengthening of the central power at the expense of the separate powers. But this Senate, as it exists, is a result of the compromise and agreement by which the various provinces now constituting the Dominion of Canada entered into' that confederation, and it seems to me it would be a very wise thing for this House and for the people of this country to hesitate a very considerable time before in the least they attempt to invalidate, alter or amend that original agreement.
There has been a number of motions before this House tending in that direction. They have all been voted down for the simple reason, in my judgment, that the most overwhelming case must be made of the necessity for such a change before this House should contemplate it or endeavour to undertake it.
The existence of the Senate is, in a measure, the existence in our constitution of that which represents the sovereignty of the different provinces. To my mind, the only reform of the Senate which would render it more effective to-day for the discharge of that duty would be making it possibly more representative of the* provinces than it is at present. It does preserve the sovereignty of the province to this extent that it gives to the various districts equal representation in the Senate and requires the members to come from these different parts. It seems to me that the framers of the constitution were wise in adopting this bi-cameral system. It has been mentioned that in all large constitutional governments since th e world began there has been a second chamber, and if there is a necessity of a second chamber in a single state, there is a double necessity in a confederation such as we have in Canada. There is the neces-

sity of having some power that can, in a measure, prevent any infringement on the sovereign rights of the provinces, which under the confederation agreement have been inserted in this British North America Act. I think further that this House does not sufficiently examine the work of the Senate, in order to find justification for it. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster) spoke of the demoralizing influences of the appointments to the Senate. I do not think any one can visit that body without finding that they are an extremely moral and respectable body.

I rise to ask my hon. friend if he thinks that is fair tactics. He surely did not understand me as saying that the men who constitute the Senate were immoral and demoralized? I would be verry sorry if he would allow that idea to go out on ' Hansard.'
The hon. gentleman said the appointments were made in a demoralizing mode, that it was practically a purchase of them.
I gave my hon. friend a chance to set himself right.

And one was that the Senate was appointed in such a manner as to demoralize the gentlemen going into the Senate. If that does not make the men immoral I do not know what does. He also spoke of it as a place filled with rancor or strife. If he visited it he would find neither rancor nor strife, it is the calmest atmosphere to be found in the world and one might almost think it the place where the wicked cease from troubling and the weary are at rest, because it is as calm and sober as it can be;/ I really believe that if members of this/ House before framing these attacks on the Senate would examine a little more carefully the work done by the Senate, they would not make so many charges. I think that before charges of that kind are made there should be an investigation into the, Senate, and it would be found that in many respects it exercises a revising and a critical influence upon this body, which is for good.
The existence of a second body is to my mind an absolute necessity in our constitution. If it had no other purpose it would serve the purpose well defined and aptly described in the very name of the Norwegian second chamber, which is called the Lagthmg. It is necessary in a country becoming so democratic as this country that we should put some checks upon ourselves in order not to rush too rapidly into hasty legislation. There is great danger in this country of every one with a little fad starting up some movement which may
get on the statute-book and in that way practically frittering away the liberty ot the subject. I believe that many of these things are saved from being placed on the statute-book of this country by the opportunity which is afforded for their consideration in a second chamber. Occasions may arise in the future, where the senatorial body will have an opportunity more largely and in a more important manner to fulfil its functions than it has had in the past. I think the fathers of confederation must have been influenced by the fact that going through the constitutions from the earliest confederation of which we have any knowledge, from the Achaean League down to the American constitution, they found all the best intellects who. had ever been engaged in framing a constitution determined and insistent on having a second chamber. I do not think we should too hastily rush away from the precedents supported by such eminent authorities as the great constitution makers of other countries as well as the able gentleman who made a Senate part of the compromise upon which our own constitution is founded.

I regret that I cannot see my way, as a matter of principle, to adopting the suggestion of the right hon. the Prime Minister Sir Wilfrid Laurier) to withdraw this motion. And, not only as a matter of principle do I feel unable to comply, but also because I have heard no'thing to-night to give me an excuse, if I were looking for one, to withdraw this motion. We have heard the Prime Minister, in a somewhat instructive address, tell us some of the history of the matter, and some of the ideas with regard to the constitution of the Senate that have been from time to time put forward. But we have not heard a suggestion from him that even now he intends to take hold of this matter which ought to have been dealt with, certainly, some time within the last fourteen years? It is idle to suppose that gentleman on the left of Mr. Speaker in this House can produce any concrete result or give effect to their suggestions unless the Prime Minister will, with his strength in this House, and in the country, take up these suggestions and undertake to give them effect. And, until somebody else- I would prefer the Prime Minister-makes a concrete motion, I am going to stick to my concrete motion.to abolish the Senate. For it seems to me there is no reason for its continued existence ; and, I think that this is pretty clearly shown even by the speeches o' the gentlemen who support the existence of the Senate. For, to be frank about it, these gentlemen have only tried to apologize for the Senate; they are driven by the stress of the argument to try to find excuses for the Senate's existence. After fourteen years there is a complete

failure to bring about a reform which the gentlemen now in power undertook to then bring about at once. And the hon. member for Yukon (Mr. Congdon) asks us, in all seriousness, to go to the Senate chamber and examine their work. Why, it would take a microscope and telescope to find it. It would need two or three people to go there and ring the bells to bring about any movement in the Senate preliminary to having any work done at all. It is because I have examined the iwork of the Senate that I realize that some reformation should be brought about. But, as I have not found any two of the bright minds of this chamber agreeing upon any particular measure of reform, it seems to me that abolition is the only thing that can reasonably be proposed, it seems to have been assumed that if this resolution passes this House, the Senate will be at once abolished. Of course, that is not the case. But, if the resolution is carried, the petition proposed would go to the King, and it would be acted upon in some way. It does not follow that tire prayer of the petition would be granted, but it does follow that some step would be made toward changing the present condition of affairs, whether in the direction of reform or in the direction of abolition. The Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) laughs. He doesn't want anything done apparently. But he knows that what I say is correct-that a motion passed in this House cannot alter the constitution of the country. Some hon. gentlemen, the Prime Minister among them, speak as if we could do something that the home government, imperial parliament could not do-that we could reform while they can only abolish. We cannot amend even in the most infinitesimal way the constitution ; that is the work of the imperial parliament.
In view of the fact that, though the whole evening has been taken up in discussing the subject no one from the Prime Minister down has said that the government intends to take a step toward a reformation that was promised before the present government came inTo office, I should be derelict in my duty if I consented to withdraw the motion.
Motion (Mr. Lancaster) negatived on division.
ADJOURNMENT-BUSINESS OF THE _ HOUSE.
Sir WILFRID LAURIER moved the adjournment of the House.
Does the Prime Minister intend to go on with Supply after the preliminaries are finished to-morrow?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
We will take up first the third readings of two Bills, those first on the list-the Bill to amend Mr. LANCASTER.
the Immigration Act and the Bill to prohibit the importation and use of opium and other drugs. After that, Supply.
And the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) knows that the hon. member for West Algoma (Mr. Boyce) intends to propose an amendment.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: Yes.

I give notice that on the first opportunity afforded on going into Supply I will move:
Tliat the recent mergers of heretofore competing industries and the issue of securities resulting therefrom should be the subject of public investigation, with a view of ascertaining how far such mergers or the methods of carrying them out affect the public interest, either as causing continuing .high prices for the commodities produced, as damaging the reputation of Canadian securities abroad or further as restricting the banking facilities of the country.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 11.25 p.m.
Tuesday, January 31, 1911.
